transcript:
User: Hello? Yeah... I got your card. You help with phones, right?
Agent: Yeah, we help with phones so you’re not losing business when nobody can pick up.  

Got it — when you say “help with phones,” what were you hoping it could do for you?
User: Uh, I just need someone to answer calls when I'm busy. Too many go to voicemail.
Agent: Got it, so it’s really about answering calls when you’re tied up so they don’t hit voicemail.  

When a call comes in and you’re out working or with a customer, who’s supposed to be picking it up right now?
User: Uh, well, usually it's just me. So, they just go to voicemail if I can't answer.
Agent: Yeah, that makes sense — so if you’re tied up, it just rings out and lands in voicemail.  

Those calls that hit voicemail now… do people usually leave a message, or do they just hang up and call the next place?
User: Uh, some leave a message, but I think a lot just hang up. Hard to keep track.
Agent: Yeah, that’s what I hear a lot — the ones who hang up are usually the ones you really want.  

Rough guess: how many calls a week do you think are hitting voicemail instead of you picking up live?
User: Uh, I don't know, a bunch, maybe ten? Fifteen? It's hard to say exactly.
Agent: Gotcha, so maybe around 10–15 a week where you’re not really sure what you missed.  

What kind of work do you do, by the way — what industry are you in?
User: Uh, I run a small landscaping business. You know, mowing lawns, planting, that kind of stuff.
Agent: Nice, thanks — landscaping’s exactly where this hurts, especially in spring when everyone’s calling at once.  

When those 10–15 calls a week hit voicemail, are you more worried about missing one-off mow jobs, or the bigger recurring maintenance contracts you could keep all season?
User: Uh, probably the bigger contracts. Those are more important to keep steady work coming in all season.
Agent: Yeah, totally makes sense — those season-long contracts are your bread and butter.  

Has anyone ever actually walked you through what those missed calls are likely costing you in contracts each month, or not really?
User: Uh, not really. I haven't thought much about it, just trying to keep up with work.
Agent: Yeah, totally get that — when you’re in the field, you’re just trying to get jobs done, not run numbers.  

Mind if we do a super quick back-of-the-napkin math on it together, just to see what you might be leaving on the table?
User: Uh, sure, I guess we can try. I'm not great with numbers, though.
Agent: No worries at all — I’ll keep it super simple.  

So ballpark, out of those calls that hit voicemail in a week, how many would you say you miss total — closer to 10 or closer to 15?
User: Uh, might be closer to 15, but it's hard to tell exactly.
Agent: Got it, let’s use 15 to keep it simple.  

Out of those missed calls, what percent do you think would actually turn into a job if you could pick up — maybe around half, or more like 60–70%?
Agent: Perfect, let’s roll with that.  

So if you’re missing about 15 calls a week and could book around 60% of them at, say, a $600 job, that’s roughly $5,400 a week — and about $23,300 a month — potentially slipping away just because they hit voicemail… does that feel in the ballpark of what you might be missing, or does it surprise you?
User: Uh, I have no idea — half? More? It's hard to say, really.
Agent: Yeah, totally fair — it’s hard to know exactly, but even a chunk of that is a lot to leave on voicemail.  

So… to actually stop that from happening and show you what your numbers look like with this turned on, would you be open to a quick 20‑minute walkthrough this week to see how many of those missed calls we can turn into jobs?
User: Uh, sure, I guess I can do that. Just need to know when and how it works.
Agent: Makes sense — we’ll keep it simple.  

Quick thing first so I book this right: what’s your first name?
User: Uh, it's Pedro. Just Pedro, nothing fancy.
Agent: Nice to meet you, Pedro.  

And what’s your last name?
User: Uh, it's Gonzalez. But just call me Pedro, everyone does.
Agent: Got it, Pedro Gonzalez, I’ll stick with Pedro.  

What’s the name of your landscaping company?
User: Uh, it's just called Pedro's Landscaping. Kept it simple.
Agent: Nice, simple is good — Pedro’s Landscaping.  

And is the number you’re calling from right now the best one to text you the appointment details, or is there a better 10‑digit number to use?
User: Uh, yeah, this number works. Just text me here with the details.
Agent: Perfect, we’ll use this number.  

Quick check — you’re on Central time, right?
User: Uh, no, I'm on Eastern time. But I can adjust if needed.
Agent: Got it, Eastern time, thanks for clearing that up.  

One moment while I check availability — would you prefer later today or tomorrow for that quick demo?
User: Uh, tomorrow might be better. I have a busy day today with some jobs lined up.
Agent: Gotcha, tomorrow’s better with the jobs you’ve got today.  

I can get you in tomorrow at either 4:15 or 5:00 in the afternoon Eastern — which works better for you?
User: Uh, 5:00 sounds good. Gives me more time to finish up.
Agent: Perfect, tomorrow at 5:00 Eastern works.  

Oh sorry, I didn’t get your number quite right — could you verify it real quick?
User: Uh, yeah, it's just this number you called. That's the one I use for everything with the business.
Agent: Mhm, thanks — I just need the actual digits so it saves correctly.  

Can you read it out for me real quick, starting with the area code?
User: Uh, sure, it's 555-123-4567. That's the business line.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that.
Agent: Thanks, Pedro. The calendar’s being a little fussy on my side, so here’s what we’ll do — we’ve got you down for tomorrow at 5:00 Eastern, and someone from our team will call you on your business line within the hour just to lock that in and confirm the details. Really glad you called in today — is there anything else you need from me right now before we hop off?
